warmup.q: A virtual thread prints Thread.currentThread(), sleeps for 50 ms, and prints it again. What do you expect to see?
options: The same platform thread both times, because a thread can't change its operating system thread
The same virtual thread both times, possibly running on a different carrier thread after the sleep
Two different virtual threads, because the JDK creates a new one after each blocking call
The carrier thread, because currentThread() returns the operating system thread that runs the code
warmup.why: Thread.currentThread() always returns the virtual thread itself, never its carrier. During the sleep the virtual thread is set aside, and when it wakes, any free carrier can pick it up. Its toString() names the current carrier after the @, which is how the demo in the second section makes the move visible.

opening:
Picture last lesson's restaurant, run differently. It keeps only four waiters, and writes each table's service on an order slip: what the table has had, and what comes next. When a table waits for the kitchen, the waiter clips its slip to a board by the kitchen door and picks up a slip that's ready. When the dish is ready, any free waiter takes that slip and carries on from its last line. Four waiters serve two hundred tables, because nobody stands at the door.

Java's virtual threads work like that restaurant. In The thread-per-request wall, 2,000 virtual threads each slept 100 ms, and the run took about 150 ms on four cores. Thread.sleep used to hold a thread for the whole wait, so something put 2,000 threads down and picked them up again, and the code never noticed.

It's tempting to picture a virtual thread as a tiny operating system thread, or a faster one. Both pictures lead to wrong guesses. In this lesson, we'll find the slip inside a virtual thread, watch threads change waiters mid-task, see where a thread lets go and weigh a waiting thread. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started in a restaurant with four waiters and a board full of order slips. A virtual thread works the same way: a Thread plus a continuation, carried by a few carrier threads, put down at a blocking call and picked up by any free carrier. Its frames wait on the heap, a few kilobytes of them.

Now look in your own code for a long loop that never calls anything that waits, such as a big calculation or parsing a large file. On a virtual thread, that loop holds its carrier until it's done.

Next, we'll put virtual threads to work, one per task. If they're this cheap, why does a database with 20 connections still need a limit?

sections.h: What a virtual thread is made of: a Thread plus a continuation
sections.html:
Start with what you can see. Thread.ofVirtual().start(task) returns an ordinary java.lang.Thread, and isVirtual() on it returns true. Inside the JDK, the object is a java.lang.VirtualThread, a subclass your code can't use directly. It holds two things that a platform thread, one backed by a thread of the operating system, doesn't have: a continuation and a scheduler.

Before we name the first one, do a small job by hand. Suppose you had to stop a method halfway and finish it tomorrow. What would you write down? The line you're on and the values of its local variables. Then the same again for the method that called it, and the one that called that, all the way up.

That list already has a name. Each method call that hasn't returned yet has a frame, a small record of its local variables and of the line to go back to. The frames, piled one on another, make the thread's stack. To pause a thread, you save its frames. To resume it, you put them back.

A continuation is exactly that: a piece of work that can stop in the middle and carry on later from the same line, with its frames intact. It's the order slip from the opening. The JDK has an internal class for it, jdk.internal.vm.Continuation, with two operations that matter here. In outline (the real class also takes a scope argument, which we skip):

cont = new Continuation(() -> { a(); yield(); b(); })
cont.run()    // runs a(), stops at yield(), returns here
cont.run()    // carries on with b()

run() starts the work, or resumes it where it stopped. yield(), called from inside the work, stops it and returns to whoever called run(), with the frames kept. The next run() carries on from the line after the yield().

You can't call this class yourself, because Java doesn't export its package. The virtual thread uses it for you. It wraps your task in a continuation, and when the task is about to block, the JDK calls yield(). The task stops, and no thread of the operating system waits for it.

The second part, the scheduler, decides which stopped continuation runs next, and on which platform thread. In the restaurant, it's the manager who decides which waiter takes which slip.

To your code, a virtual thread is just a thread. Thread.currentThread() returns it, ThreadLocals (variables with a separate value for each thread) work, interrupt() works, and sleep throws InterruptedException the same way. A few things differ, all listed in the Thread Javadoc. Virtual threads are always daemon threads, which the JVM doesn't wait for when the program ends. Their priority is fixed, they have no name unless you give one, and Thread.getAllStackTraces() leaves them out.

A slip needs someone to carry it, though. In the JDK, that someone is called a carrier.

sections.h: Mount, unmount, mount again: how a few carriers run every virtual thread
sections.html:
The default scheduler is a ForkJoinPool, the pool from the executors track whose threads take work from each other's queues. The JDK creates one just for virtual threads, separate from ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), which parallel streams use. It works first in, first out, so ready virtual threads run roughly in the order they became ready.

Its workers are platform threads, and they have a name of their own: carrier threads. By default there's one per core, a part of the processor that runs one thread at a time (Runtime.availableProcessors() gives the count, and -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=N changes it). The carriers are the restaurant's four waiters.

Two words describe a virtual thread's life on a carrier. To mount is to start running a virtual thread on a carrier. The carrier takes a ready virtual thread and runs its continuation, so the thread's top frames sit on the carrier's own stack. To unmount is the reverse. At a blocking call, the continuation yields and its frames are copied to the heap, the memory where Java keeps its objects. The carrier goes back for the next ready thread.

Let's trace the smallest case: two carriers, C1 and C2, and three virtual threads.

  • VT1 and VT2 are ready at the same moment. C1 mounts VT1, and C2 mounts VT2.
  • VT1 calls sleep(50). It unmounts, its frames go to the heap, and C1 is free.
  • VT3 arrives a moment later. C1 mounts it while VT1 sleeps.
  • VT2 finishes, so C2 is free. VT1's 50 ms run out, and it goes back in the queue.
  • C2 mounts VT1, which carries on after sleep. It started on C1 and finishes on C2.

That move is normal: a virtual thread that unmounts can come back on any carrier. CarrierDemo, in the Try it below, makes it visible. It starts 8 virtual threads that each print Thread.currentThread(), sleep 50 ms, and print it again. A virtual thread's toString() names its carrier after the @. On this 4-core machine, while other programs were busy, one run printed this (three of the eight rows):

before: VirtualThread[#19,checkout-0]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1  after: VirtualThread[#19,checkout-0]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3
before: VirtualThread[#22,checkout-1]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2  after: VirtualThread[#22,checkout-1]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2
before: VirtualThread[#24,checkout-2]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1  after: VirtualThread[#24,checkout-2]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3

8 virtual threads ran on 3 carrier threads [ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1, ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2, ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3] (this machine has 4 cores).
7 of them woke up on a different carrier than the one they slept on.
All 8 finished after 109 ms.

Seven of the eight woke up on a different carrier, and not one of them was told.

The carrier is hidden from your code on purpose. Thread.currentThread() returns the virtual thread, never the carrier, and the carrier's own ThreadLocals are out of reach. If they weren't, a value one checkout left on a carrier would leak into whichever checkout mounted there next. The @ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3 part of toString() is there for debugging only, and its format isn't specified anywhere.

So the restaurant holds up: the slip never knows which waiter carries it, and it doesn't need to.

A virtual thread can come back on any carrier after every blocking call. Never write code that cares which one.

Check yourself: a virtual thread runs a task that sleeps three times and then returns. How many times does its continuation yield, and how many times is it mounted? It yields three times, once per sleep. It's mounted four times: once to start, and once after each sleep.

So far our threads only slept. Which other calls let a thread put its slip down, and which don't?

try.title: Watch virtual threads change carriers
steps: Run CarrierDemo with the command below. It starts 8 virtual threads that print Thread.currentThread(), sleep 50 ms, and print it again.
Count the carriers in the summary line, and compare that with your number of cores. How many threads woke up on a different carrier?
Predict, then run with one carrier: -Pargs='8 1'. Does it take 8 times as long?

code.title: CarrierDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.vthreads.l02; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.TreeSet; /** * Starts some virtual threads that each print the thread they run on, sleep, and print it again. * A virtual thread's toString() shows its carrier after the '@'. * * <p>Args: number of virtual threads (default 8), and optionally the scheduler's parallelism. */ public class CarrierDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int n = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 8; if (args.length > 1) { // must be set before the first virtual thread is created System.setProperty("jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism", args[1]); } String[] before = new String[n]; String[] after = new String[n]; List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { int id = i; threads.add(Thread.ofVirtual().name("checkout-" + id).start(() -> { before[id] = Thread.currentThread().toString(); try { Thread.sleep(50); // a blocking call: the thread unmounts here } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } after[id] = Thread.currentThread().toString(); })); } for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; Set<String> carriers = new TreeSet<>(); int moved = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { System.out.printf("before: %-63s after: %s%n", before[i], after[i]); carriers.add(carrier(before[i])); carriers.add(carrier(after[i])); if (!carrier(before[i]).equals(carrier(after[i]))) moved++; } System.out.printf("%n%d virtual threads ran on %d carrier threads %s (this machine has %d cores).%n", n, carriers.size(), carriers, Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()); System.out.printf("%d of them woke up on a different carrier than the one they slept on.%n", moved); System.out.printf("All %d finished after %d ms.%n", n, ms); System.out.println("Thread.currentThread().isVirtual() inside them: " + threads.get(0).isVirtual() + ", daemon: " + threads.get(0).isDaemon()); } // "VirtualThread[#22,checkout-0]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3" -> "ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3" static String carrier(String s) { int at = s.lastIndexOf('@'); return at < 0 ? "(not mounted)" : s.substring(at + 1); } }

alt.title: CarrierDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.vthreads.l02 import java.util.TreeSet /** * Starts some virtual threads that each print the thread they run on, sleep, and print it again. * A virtual thread's toString() shows its carrier after the '@'. * * Args: number of virtual threads (default 8), and optionally the scheduler's parallelism. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val n = args.getOrNull(0)?.toInt() ?: 8 // must be set before the first virtual thread is created args.getOrNull(1)?.let { System.setProperty("jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism", it) } val before = arrayOfNulls<String>(n) val after = arrayOfNulls<String>(n) val t0 = System.nanoTime() val threads = (0 until n).map { id -> Thread.ofVirtual().name("checkout-$id").start { before[id] = Thread.currentThread().toString() try { Thread.sleep(50) // a blocking call: the thread unmounts here } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } after[id] = Thread.currentThread().toString() } } threads.forEach { it.join() } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 val carriers = TreeSet<String>() var moved = 0 for (i in 0 until n) { println("before: %-63s after: %s".format(before[i], after[i])) carriers += carrierOf(before[i]!!) carriers += carrierOf(after[i]!!) if (carrierOf(before[i]!!) != carrierOf(after[i]!!)) moved++ } println("\n$n virtual threads ran on ${carriers.size} carrier threads $carriers (this machine has ${Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()} cores).") println("$moved of them woke up on a different carrier than the one they slept on.") println("All $n finished after $ms ms.") println("Thread.currentThread().isVirtual() inside them: ${threads[0].isVirtual}, daemon: ${threads[0].isDaemon}") } // "VirtualThread[#22,checkout-0]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3" -> "ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3" private fun carrierOf(s: String): String { val at = s.lastIndexOf('@') return if (at < 0) "(not mounted)" else s.substring(at + 1) }

try.expect: On a 4-core machine the 8 virtual threads share up to four carriers, worker-1 to worker-4, and most of them wake up on a different carrier than they slept on (7 of 8 in runs here). With one carrier every line shows worker-1, and the run still takes about 50 ms plus start-up (126 ms on this busy machine). The 8 sleeps overlap, because a sleeping virtual thread doesn't hold its carrier.

aside.title: Can I see these threads in a thread dump?
aside.html: Partly. A thread dump is a snapshot of every thread and what it's doing, and the lesson A thread's life took one with jcmd <pid> Thread.print. That dump shows the carriers, as platform threads named ForkJoinPool-1-worker-N, but it doesn't list the virtual threads themselves. The JDK has a newer kind of dump for them: jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json threads.json writes the virtual threads too, grouped by the executor that started them. (jcmd is a tool that comes with the JDK, and <pid> is the number the operating system gives your running program.) With 50,000 virtual threads that file gets long, which is one more reason to name the threads you care about.

video.title: Virtual threads mount on carriers, unmount at a blocking call, and come back on any carrier

sections.h: Where a virtual thread lets go, and where it holds on
sections.html:
Unmounting isn't magic inside the JVM. The JDK team rewrote the blocking parts of Java's class library. Each one now checks whether the current thread is virtual and, if it is, yields instead of blocking. Here is parkNanos, the method underneath sleep, from java.lang.VirtualThread, trimmed to its core:

// simplified from java.lang.VirtualThread.parkNanos (JDK 25)
void parkNanos(long nanos) {
    timeout = nanos;
    setState(TIMED_PARKING);
    boolean yielded = yieldContinuation();   // unmount: frames to the heap, carrier is free
    if (!yielded) {
        parkOnCarrierThread(true, nanos);    // couldn't unmount: block the carrier instead
    }
}

First the method notes the timeout and the thread's new state, and the JDK arranges a timer that will make the thread ready again. Then yieldContinuation() unmounts it. The tricky line is the last one. If the thread can't unmount, it blocks its carrier instead, just as a platform thread would.

These operations unmount a virtual thread:

  • Thread.sleep, and LockSupport.park with everything built on it: ReentrantLock, Semaphore, CountDownLatch, BlockingQueue.take and Future.get.
  • Network reads and writes on sockets, including the JDK's HttpClient, its class for calling web services, and database drivers that use plain sockets. The JDK switches the socket to a mode where it never blocks and hands it to a poller, a part of the JDK that watches many sockets at once. Then it parks the virtual thread until data arrives.
  • From JDK 24 (JEP 491), synchronized and Object.wait(). On JDK 21 to 23, these pin the virtual thread instead: it stays mounted, and its carrier blocks with it.

Some operations can't unmount. Most file reads and writes block inside the operating system, so the virtual thread keeps its carrier for the whole call. The scheduler adds a temporary extra carrier to make up for it, up to 256 by default. Blocking while a native method (one written in C, say) or a class's static initializer, the code that sets up a class the first time it's used, is on the stack pins the carrier. Lesson 4 of this track is about pinning, and how to find it.

The last rule surprises people. Let's replace the sleep in CarrierDemo with 50 ms of busy work, a loop that just watches the clock. Predict first: eight 50 ms loops on one carrier should take about 400 ms, and on four carriers about 100 ms. Here is the end of a one-carrier run, on the busy machine:

0 of them woke up on a different carrier than the one they slept on.
All 8 finished after 532 ms.

A second one-carrier run took 415 ms, and two runs on four carriers took 172 and 155 ms. The loops ran one after another, with the busy machine adding its share. And no thread changed carrier, because none of them ever blocked, so none of them ever unmounted.

There's no time slicing for virtual threads. The operating system takes turns among its threads every few milliseconds, but nothing takes a carrier away from a virtual thread that's computing. The scheduler never taps a busy thread on the shoulder.

In the restaurant, it's a waiter chopping onions: the slip stays in his pocket until the chopping is done. Here the picture breaks a little. A real manager would send a second waiter to help. The scheduler doesn't, so four waiters chopping leave every other slip on the rail.

Virtual threads make waiting cheap, not computing. A thread that never blocks keeps its carrier.

Each time a thread does put its slip down, though, its frames have to go somewhere. Where, and what do they weigh?

try.title: Replace the sleep with real work
steps: In CarrierDemo.java, replace Thread.sleep(50); with a 50 ms busy loop: long end = System.nanoTime() + 50_000_000; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { }. The compiler then complains that nothing in the try can throw InterruptedException, so remove the try and catch too. In CarrierDemo.kt the loop is val end = System.nanoTime() + 50_000_000; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { }, and Kotlin doesn't mind the leftover catch.
Predict the total time with one carrier (-Pargs='8 1') and with the default number of carriers. Then run both.
Look at the before and after carriers. Did any thread change carrier this time?
try.expect: With one carrier the 8 loops run one after another: about 400 ms on an idle machine (415 and 532 ms in busy runs here). With 4 carriers it takes about 100 ms (155 and 172 ms here), more if other programs are busy. No thread changes carrier, because none of them ever blocks, so none of them ever unmounts. Computing is limited by carriers, which means cores.

sections.h: Where the saved stack lives, and what it weighs
sections.html:
A platform thread's stack is a fixed block of memory reserved when the thread starts. It's 1 MB by default on 64-bit Linux, whether the thread goes three calls deep or three hundred. A virtual thread's stack works differently. When it unmounts, the JDK copies its frames off the carrier's stack into stack chunk objects on the heap. A chunk is only as big as the frames really there. The garbage collector, the part of the JVM that frees memory nobody uses any more, looks after it like any other object.

When the virtual thread mounts again, the JDK doesn't copy the whole stack back. It copies the top few frames, enough to carry on. If the code returns into a frame that's still on the heap, the JDK copies more at that moment. So a thread parked deep inside a library pays for its depth when it parks, not all over again each time it wakes.

StackOnHeapDemo, in the Try it below, weighs it. It parks 10,000 virtual threads one call deep, measures the heap, lets them go, and does the same 200 calls deep. Predict: will the deep ones cost 200 times as much? One run printed:

depth   1: 10,000 parked virtual threads use about 22 MB of heap (2,344 bytes each)
depth 200: 10,000 parked virtual threads use about 95 MB of heap (10,012 bytes each)

Not 200 times: about four times. The Thread object and its bookkeeping are a fixed part of every parked thread, and each frame of this small method is small. At 1,000 calls deep, another run gave 27,085 bytes each, still about a fortieth of the megabyte a platform thread reserves up front.

Those numbers are what make a million virtual threads possible. On the restaurant's board, a slip with long notes takes more room than a short one, but no slip needs a table of its own.

The heap also explains a difference from Kotlin. A coroutine saves only the local variables of its suspend functions, in objects the compiler writes for it. A virtual thread saves the whole real stack, so a blocking call deep inside an old library, written before virtual threads existed, can still unmount. The compare block below shows both side by side.

A parked virtual thread costs heap in proportion to its real stack. Nothing is reserved for the worst case.

In the lab you build the other half of the machine: a tiny scheduler with a ready queue, a timer queue and one carrier. It mounts and unmounts continuations written by hand.

try.title: Weigh a parked virtual thread
steps: Run StackOnHeapDemo. It parks 10,000 virtual threads at call depth 1, measures the heap, releases them, then does the same at depth 200.
Before you look: how many times bigger will the depth-200 number be?
Run it with -Pargs=1000 for depth 1,000, and compare with the 1 MB a platform thread reserves.

code.title: StackOnHeapDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.vthreads.l02; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; /** * Parks 10,000 virtual threads at a chosen call depth and measures how much heap they use. * A parked virtual thread keeps its stack frames in heap objects, so deeper stacks cost more heap. * * <p>Args: call depth before parking (default: runs 1 and 200). */ public class StackOnHeapDemo { static final int THREADS = 10_000; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int[] depths = args.length > 0 ? new int[] {Integer.parseInt(args[0])} : new int[] {1, 200}; for (int depth : depths) measure(depth); } static void measure(int depth) throws InterruptedException { long base = usedHeap(); CountDownLatch parked = new CountDownLatch(THREADS); CountDownLatch release = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(THREADS); for (int i = 0; i < THREADS; i++) { threads.add(Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> descend(depth, parked, release))); } parked.await(); // every thread is now parked at the bottom of its stack long used = usedHeap() - base; System.out.printf("depth %3d: %,d parked virtual threads use about %,d MB of heap (%,d bytes each)%n", depth, THREADS, used / (1024 * 1024), used / THREADS); release.countDown(); for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); } // each level adds one stack frame; at the bottom the thread blocks and unmounts static int descend(int depth, CountDownLatch parked, CountDownLatch release) { if (depth > 1) return descend(depth - 1, parked, release) + 1; parked.countDown(); try { release.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return 0; } static long usedHeap() throws InterruptedException { Runtime rt = Runtime.getRuntime(); for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { System.gc(); Thread.sleep(50); } return rt.totalMemory() - rt.freeMemory(); } }

alt.title: StackOnHeapDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.vthreads.l02 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch /** * Parks 10,000 virtual threads at a chosen call depth and measures how much heap they use. * A parked virtual thread keeps its stack frames in heap objects, so deeper stacks cost more heap. * * Args: call depth before parking (default: runs 1 and 200). */ private const val THREADS = 10_000 fun main(args: Array<String>) { val depths = args.getOrNull(0)?.let { listOf(it.toInt()) } ?: listOf(1, 200) for (depth in depths) measure(depth) } private fun measure(depth: Int) { val base = usedHeap() val parked = CountDownLatch(THREADS) val release = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(THREADS) { Thread.ofVirtual().start { descend(depth, parked, release) } } parked.await() // every thread is now parked at the bottom of its stack val used = usedHeap() - base println("depth %3d: %,d parked virtual threads use about %,d MB of heap (%,d bytes each)" .format(depth, THREADS, used / (1024 * 1024), used / THREADS)) release.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } } // each level adds one stack frame; at the bottom the thread blocks and unmounts private fun descend(depth: Int, parked: CountDownLatch, release: CountDownLatch): Int { if (depth > 1) return descend(depth - 1, parked, release) + 1 parked.countDown() try { release.await() } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } return 0 } private fun usedHeap(): Long { val rt = Runtime.getRuntime() repeat(2) { System.gc() Thread.sleep(50) } return rt.totalMemory() - rt.freeMemory() }

try.expect: At depth 1 each parked virtual thread costs about 2 KB of heap (2,184 to 2,344 bytes in runs here). At depth 200 it costs about 10 KB, depending on the JDK and on whether the JIT, the part of the JVM that compiles busy code while it runs, has compiled descend yet. Even at depth 1,000 it stays far below 1 MB (about 27 KB here). The heap grows with the real depth of the stack, nothing more. The numbers are rough, because totalMemory - freeMemory after System.gc() is a rough measure.

compare.title: Stackful virtual threads and stackless coroutines

java.title: Java: the JDK saves the real stack
java.html: // any method can block, even deep inside an old library void checkout(Basket b) throws InterruptedException { Payment paid = bank.charge(b); // a blocking network read: unmounts here Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(30)); // unmounts here too orders.save(b, paid); // a plain database call over a socket: unmounts } // run it on a virtual thread; nothing in checkout() knows Thread.ofVirtual().name("checkout-", 0).start(() -> { try { checkout(basket); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } });

kotlin.title: Kotlin: the compiler builds a state machine
kotlin.html: // only suspend calls can pause; the compiler rewrites this function suspend fun checkout(b: Basket) { val paid = bank.charge(b) // must be a suspend fun to free the thread delay(30) orders.save(b, paid) // a blocking database call here would block the thread } // roughly what the compiler generates (simplified): // class CheckoutContinuation(var label: Int, var paid: Payment?) // label 0: call charge(b); label = 1; return COROUTINE_SUSPENDED // label 1: paid = result; call delay(30); label = 2; return COROUTINE_SUSPENDED // label 2: orders.save(b, paid)

compare.note: Both pause in the middle of a function and carry on later, possibly on another thread. Kotlin coroutines are stackless: the compiler turns each suspend function into a state machine, a class with a counter that says which step comes next, and keeps its local variables in fields. So only suspend calls can pause. Virtual threads are stackful: the JVM copies the real frames, so any blocking JDK call anywhere on the stack can unmount, even inside a library compiled before virtual threads existed. The fibers in this lesson's lab are written by hand in the Kotlin style, with a counter, so you can see what the JDK saves you from writing.

worked.title: Follow one checkout through a sleep

steps.say: Here is the task. The numbered comments mark the points where the virtual thread's life changes. (sleepQuietly is a small helper that calls Thread.sleep and handles the interrupt, so the Java lambda stays short.)
steps.code: Thread vt = Thread.ofVirtual().name("checkout-1").start(() -> { // 1. start: queued in the scheduler Stock stock = warehouse.reserve(basket); // 2. mounted on some carrier, say worker-2 sleepQuietly(Duration.ofMillis(50)); // 3. unmounts here; worker-2 is free bank.charge(basket, stock); // 4. resumed, maybe on worker-4 });

alt.html: val vt = Thread.ofVirtual().name("checkout-1").start { // 1. start: queued in the scheduler val stock = warehouse.reserve(basket) // 2. mounted on some carrier, say worker-2 Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(50)) // 3. unmounts here; worker-2 is free bank.charge(basket, stock) // 4. resumed, maybe on worker-4 }

steps.say: Start. start() runs nothing on the caller's thread. It puts the virtual thread's continuation in the scheduler's queue as a task, and the caller carries on at once.

Mount. A free carrier, worker-2, takes the task and calls run() on the continuation. The frames of the lambda and of warehouse.reserve now sit on worker-2's stack, and inside them Thread.currentThread() is checkout-1. The network reads inside warehouse.reserve may unmount and mount it again several times on their own.

Unmount. sleep reaches parkNanos, which arranges a timer for 50 ms and calls yieldContinuation(). The JDK copies the frames into a stack chunk on the heap, and run() returns on worker-2. worker-2 goes back to the queue and mounts another virtual thread. No operating system thread is blocked.

Wake and mount again. The timer fires and makes checkout-1 ready, which puts its continuation back in the queue. Whichever carrier is free next, say worker-4, mounts it and copies the top frames back, and sleep returns. The code calls bank.charge without knowing it moved.

lab.title: Build a one-carrier scheduler
steps: Read Fiber and Step. A Fiber is a continuation written by hand: each resume() runs to the next blocking point and returns Step.Sleep(ms) or Step.Done. You don't change these two files.
Run the tests once. All six fail. Read ToySchedulerTest.sleeper: it's a fiber written as a state machine, with a counter that says which step comes next, like a Kotlin suspend function.
In ToyScheduler, add a ready queue (ArrayDeque<Fiber>), a timer queue (a PriorityQueue of a small record holding the wake-up time, a sequence number and the fiber), and a long now.

Write run() as one loop that runs while either queue has something. If nothing is ready, jump now to the earliest wake-up and move every fiber due at that time into the ready queue. Then take one ready fiber, count a mount, call resume(), and put it in the timer queue if it asked to sleep.
Run the tests until all six pass. Look at the 10,000-fiber test: 30,000 mounts on one thread, and the clock ends at 150 ms.
hints: Order the timer queue by wake-up time, then by a sequence number you increase on every park. That keeps fibers that wake at the same moment in the order they went to sleep.
Java 21 can switch on the sealed Step: switch (step) { case Step.Sleep s -> ...; case Step.Done d -> { } }. The compiler checks that you covered both.
Move fibers out of the timer queue only when the ready queue is empty. Running code takes no virtual time, so the clock moves only when nothing can run.

drill.title: The scheduler loop from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. On paper or in a blank file, write the body of run(): a ready queue, a timer queue ordered by wake-up time, a virtual clock, and the mount and unmount steps. Then label each part with the real thing it stands for in the JDK (the ForkJoinPool's queue, the carrier, yield(), the timer that wakes a sleeping thread).

answer.html: int mounts = 0; while (!ready.isEmpty() || !sleeping.isEmpty()) { if (ready.isEmpty()) { // JDK: carriers idle, waiting for events now = sleeping.peek().wakeAt(); while (!sleeping.isEmpty() && sleeping.peek().wakeAt() <= now) { ready.addLast(sleeping.poll().fiber()); // JDK: the timer unparks, thread is resubmitted } } Fiber f = ready.pollFirst(); // JDK: a carrier takes the next task (FIFO) mounts++; Step step = f.resume(); // JDK: mount, Continuation.run() if (step instanceof Step.Sleep s) { // JDK: Continuation.yield() at sleep, unmount sleeping.add(new Parked(now + s.millis(), seq++, f)); } } return mounts;

alt.html: var mounts = 0 while (ready.isNotEmpty() || sleeping.isNotEmpty()) { if (ready.isEmpty()) { // JDK: carriers idle, waiting for events now = sleeping.peek().wakeAt while (sleeping.isNotEmpty() && sleeping.peek().wakeAt <= now) { ready.addLast(sleeping.poll().fiber) // JDK: the timer unparks, thread is resubmitted } } val f = ready.removeFirst() // JDK: a carrier takes the next task (FIFO) mounts++ when (val step = f.resume()) { // JDK: mount, Continuation.run() is Step.Sleep -> sleeping.add(Parked(now + step.millis(), seq++, f)) // JDK: yield() at sleep, unmount is Step.Done -> {} } } return mounts

recap: A virtual thread is a Thread whose task runs inside a continuation: work that can stop at yield() and carry on later with its frames intact.

Carrier threads are the platform-thread workers of a ForkJoinPool made for virtual threads, one per core by default. Mount means a carrier runs the virtual thread; unmount means it lets go at a blocking call.
Thread.currentThread() always returns the virtual thread. A virtual thread may come back on a different carrier after every blocking call.
Sleep, park (locks, queues, latches, futures) and socket I/O unmount. synchronized unmounts from JDK 24 only. File I/O holds on to the carrier, and native frames pin it.
The limit: there is no time slicing. A virtual thread that computes keeps its carrier until it blocks or ends.
A parked virtual thread's frames live on the heap in stack chunks sized to the real depth, about 2 KB for a shallow stack.

explain.prompt: A friend asks: "If a virtual thread is a real Thread, how can a million of them run on 8 operating system threads? Doesn't Thread.sleep block the thread?" Explain what happens to a virtual thread when it sleeps.
explain.answer: A virtual thread runs its task inside a continuation, on a carrier thread taken from a small ForkJoinPool, about one per core. When the code calls sleep, the JDK sees that the current thread is virtual. It sets a timer and yields the continuation: the stack frames are copied to the heap, and the carrier goes back to run another virtual thread. No operating system thread waits. When the timer fires, the virtual thread goes back into the queue, and whichever carrier is free mounts it, copies the top frames back, and sleep returns. So a million sleeping virtual threads are a million small heap objects, and only the ones actually running need a carrier. The same happens for socket reads, locks and queues, but not for long computations, which keep the carrier until they finish.

deeper.html:
Three details of the machinery are worth knowing, because they explain behavior you'll see in real programs.

How sockets unmount. A socket used from a virtual thread is put in non-blocking mode, where a read returns at once even when no data has arrived. When a read would have to wait, the JDK hands the socket to its poller and parks the virtual thread. The poller uses the operating system's way of waiting on many sockets at once (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS) and wakes each virtual thread when its socket is ready. One wait covers thousands of connections, which is what event-loop libraries do by hand.

Why file I/O is different. Linux has no general non-blocking way to read regular files that the JDK uses here, so a file read really blocks the operating system thread. The JDK lets the virtual thread keep its carrier for the whole call, and asks the scheduler for a temporary extra carrier so the other virtual threads keep running. That's why jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize exists. A program that does heavy file I/O on virtual threads can see the carrier count grow toward 256.

Why first in, first out. A ForkJoinPool normally runs a worker's own newest task first, which suits splitting a big job into pieces. For virtual threads the JDK creates it in async mode, which runs tasks first in, first out, so a virtual thread that became ready long ago runs before one that became ready a moment ago. That keeps waits fair across requests.

The scheduler itself is not a public API in JDK 21 or 25. You can tune its size with the system properties, but you can't plug in a scheduler of your own. Libraries that need special scheduling still use platform threads.
